explanations.explanation: This neuron is simply detecting the Unicode “replacement” character (U+FFFD, the little black-diamond-question-mark glyph) – i.e. bad/unknown‐encoding tokens that show up as “�” in the text.
This neuron flags section‐heading/title boundaries—i.e. it spikes on the first tokens of headlines, captions, menu labels, section titles or other standalone titles that open a new block of content.

This feature detects “boilerplate” or interface‐level tokens used to structure or navigate content—things like section prompts (“Continue Reading Below”), call-to-action buttons (“Take Action Now”), column or field labels (“Total Cost”), metadata stamps or dates (“Oct 15”), form-field cues (“Enter Your Name”), address/postcode fragments (“SW 1P”), and even horizontal separators in code or docs.

This neuron fires on the last word (often a proper noun, date‐abbrev, price, caption credit, etc.) of a standalone heading or title‐like snippet—i.e. the token that closes a headline/caption/paper‐title or other top‐of‐text label just before the main body starts.

This neuron is picking out the little “glue” characters that break up technical identifiers and data‐format strings—dots in package names and URLs, slashes in schemas and dates, the “T” in ISO timestamps, hex‐digit segments inside GUIDs, etc. It’s a delimiter/segment‐marker detector in code/JSON/XML contexts.
This feature fires on capitalized words that kick off standalone segments—titles, headlines or sentence-initial tokens—serving as a signal that you’re at the start of a new section or thought.
This feature picks out tokens that mark an interval or span—especially slashes and dashes (and related words like “early”) used to join dates, seasons, decades or other numeric ranges.

This feature fires on the point where a new label or term is being introduced—either the first word of a section/title or the acronym in a parenthetical definition. In other words, it marks tokens that serve as the “name tag” for a key method, measure or concept (e.g. the opening word of a heading like “Expression” or “Simple,” or the acronym when it’s first defined, as in “liquid–liquid extraction (LLE)” or “multidimensional LC (MDLC)”).

This feature marks the leading subword (the “first chunk”) of multi-subword proper names and entity labels—whether people, places, species, legal opinions, product titles, etc.—across languages and domains.

This feature fires on the little “titles” or labels that kick off new sections or list‐items in a document—those standalone, often capitalized words (or abbreviations like “Sept.”) and their trailing punctuation that mark the start of a heading or bullet entry (e.g. “Services,” “News,” “company history,” “only.”).

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the short, title- or headline-style phrases that kick off articles, posts or sections (e.g. “Flu shot…,” “6 Ways to Cope…,” “Newcastle United 0-1…,” “El Pack de Kimberly…,” etc.), marking the start of a news headline, blog post title or similar heading.
This neuron fires on the lead‐in to noun phrases—e.g. definite articles (“the”), possessives (“their,” “our”), adjectives (“new,” “broken”) or proper nouns (“Ethiopia”) that mark the start of an NP.

This feature lights up on “binding/definition” markers across contexts—e.g. the natural‐language verbs “is” or “be” in math statements, the assignment operator `=` in code and XML/ORM declarations, the equality test `==`, and the type‐arrow/colon syntax (`->`, `::`) in Haskell.

This neuron is a detector for in‐line punctuation markers—especially non–sentence-ending periods and similar symbols that signal abbreviations, initials, decimal points, corporate suffixes, comment delimiters or parenthetical attributions (e.g. “U.S.”, “St.”, “Feb.”, “225.5”, “Inc.”, “/*”, “(Reuters)”).

This feature is a detector for the hyphen/minus “–” token, registering when “–” appears (often between letters or digits) as a separator in hyphenated words, numeric ranges (dates, codes), regex patterns, file-version strings, etc.

This feature flags the period‐dot when it’s used as an orthographic marker in abbreviations or version/decimal separators (e.g. “Minn.”, “Inc.”, “4.01”, “3.2”) across code, markup and legal/news headers.
This neuron is a subword‐level “name chunk” detector—it lights up on the little syllable pieces (eter, eric, yan, mar, ita, etc.) that commonly occur inside personal names across languages.

This feature fires on tokens that serve as the left‐hand endpoint of numeric ranges or interval expressions—i.e. the first number (or number‐word) in hyphenated or parenthesized spans (often with units) that define value ranges, durations or measures.

This feature is firing on the literal “**” token—the double‐asterisk punctuation used as a comment-block or Markdown-style delimiter (bold markers, doc-comment line prefixes, license-header adornments) across code and legal/metadata headers.

This neuron fires on tokens that are parts of names and titles—especially the leading subword or small function‐word inside multiword proper nouns (people, places, organizations, book‐ or movie‐titles).
This feature fires on the token that ends a title or section‐heading—i.e. the boundary marker between a headline/label (in papers, patents, blogs, etc.) and the start of the main text.

explanations.explanation: This neuron seems to mark sentence-level adverbials and stance/emphasis modifiers—words that signal degree, narrative pacing or speaker attitude (e.g. just, really, quite, absolutely, ultimately, back as “return”).

This feature fires on formal document preambles—those boilerplate header lines that label a text’s metadata (e.g. case names & citations, court or DOCTYPE declarations, copyright/license comment blocks) at the very start of legal filings or source files.

This neuron fires on little “glue” words and marks that join or relate parts of a sentence—coordinating conjunctions (“and,” и, і), conditional markers (если), Japanese postpositions/case particles (から, が), even boundary punctuation—i.e. on tokens that syntactically connect or link clauses across languages.

This feature detects high-level “label” or “declaration” tokens that introduce the type or category of a document or section—e.g. LaTeX’s \documentclass, the word “median” in a stats header, “dump” in dumpster‐rental ads, “opens” in open-source URLs, “dictionary” in XML, etc.

This neuron fires on the very first token of a structured heading or title—e.g. the volume number in a case citation (426, 843, 238 F.3d), the “UNPUBLISHED” banner, or the opening word of a paper (“Disproportionation”). In other words, it flags the start‐of‐section header in formal, highly formatted documents.

This feature fires on the paired delimiter + identifier sequences that kick off named or labeled blocks—e.g. comment/open‐brace plus key in JSON, “#” plus word in Markdown, `module`/`exports` or `require` in JS, file-extension tags, LeetCode problem numbers, etc.—i.e. the syntax that marks the start of a new structural declaration across code, markup, and docs.

This feature marks the onset of semantically important words—especially nouns and names—by firing on subword pieces (often capitalized or domain‐specific prefixes) that begin contentful tokens across multiple languages.

This feature fires on the “. ” in the abbreviation “No.” that introduces docket or case numbers in U.S. court‐opinion headings—it picks out the punctuation marking the “No.” prefix before a case’s reference number.

This neuron fires on the very first token of a self-standing header or prologue—i.e. the opening word or marker that kicks off a new top-level section (case caption, article title, product name, code-file header, social post, HTML doctype, etc.).

This neuron flags the switch from normal text into a code or shell snippet in technical (e.g. StackOverflow) writing—it lights up on the colon that introduces a code block and on the very first token of that block (command names, identifiers or acronyms like “em” in emulator, “ev” in evtest, “v” for version, “g” in ggplot2, “QU” in jQuery, “ENV” in ENVIRONMENT, “Visual” in Visual Studio, “emph” in LaTeX, etc.).
This neuron fires on the very first, title‐cased word of a new headline or section—i.e. it marks the start of a document or heading by detecting that initial capitalized token.

This feature fires on structural “edge” tokens that mark the start or end of a text segment—e.g. the /* … */ comment delimiters in code, sentence‐terminating punctuation (., …, 。), and the leading words of headings or titles.

This feature lights up on the little “list-starter” or “item-connector” words in formal prose—tokens that introduce or join off enumerated elements (e.g. “the following” in licenses, “as well as”/“and” in descriptions, or technical list markers like “chain” in “polymerase chain reaction” or “IL” in cytokine panels).

This feature lights up on the tokens that mark the start of a new structural section or metadata header—things like article titles or section headings (“News,” “Biographical Information,” “Studie,” “Grant No.”), wiki/categorization lines, code‐comment delimiters (“/*”), and similar document‐boundary markers.

This neuron fires on “structural” markers that open or separate units of text—e.g. declaration keywords in code (import, DECLARE), bracketed identifiers in SQL, doc-comment tags (param), measurement or list bullets (numbers, “a”/“the”/“to”), and punctuation (commas). In other words, it flags the tokens that signal the start of a new statement, field, or clause across code, queries, recipes, and prose.

This neuron is essentially a detector for Markdown‐style “strong” emphasis markers (the double‐asterisk tokens), which typically enclose section titles, headings or other bolded phrases (e.g. article titles, menu labels, patent or paper headings, blog post titles, etc.) across diverse text genres.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is simply picking out two‐character subword tokens—either a pair of uppercase letters or a pair of digits—so it lights up on fragments like “AV,” “WK,” “EC,” “ER” in names and on “41,” “26,” “15,” etc., in numeric codes or identifiers.
This feature marks the sentence-terminal period in standalone header or metadata lines (e.g. the final “.” ending a copyright notice, file-level comment, section title, DOCTYPE, etc.).

This neuron fires on the “key” word that names a domain‐defining phrase or entity in a Wiki‐style article—the head of a multiword proper noun or section label (e.g. the critical word in team/place/league names, study titles, cast listings, code snippet headings, etc.) that immediately tells you what sort of page or passage you’re reading.
